digests.narrative:
Everything the theme was arguing about is now filed. Lumentum reported $1.01B, up 109% year on year, and crossed 50% non-GAAP gross margin a full quarter ahead of its own target, guiding the next quarter to $1.225-1.275B. Coherent reported a record $2.05B, up 34%, with datacenter and communications at 79% of revenue and up 59%, six-inch indium phosphide capacity doubled ahead of plan, and the next quarter guided to $2.2-2.4B. MACOM reported $342.2M, up 35.8%, guided to $415-425M on a record 1.6 book-to-bill. Applied Optoelectronics reported $191.9M, up 86%, and returned to a $0.06 non-GAAP profit. Four companies, four beats, and the group sold off — the same reaction Cisco and Applied Materials drew in the same week.

The sorting mechanism the desk should now use is the margin ladder, because it separates these companies far more cleanly than the theme does. MACOM guides adjusted gross margin to 60-61%. Lumentum guides just above 50%. Coherent guides 39.5-41.5%. AOI guides 29-30.5%. Content sold into the module earns roughly double what assembling the module earns, and that gap is structural rather than cyclical. It also explains why the market punished the group on margin guidance while the revenue lines were record-setting.

One reading of the chokepoint needs revising. Lumentum hitting its margin target early while shipping record 800G and starting 1.6T production means internal laser capacity is scaling faster than planned — so the merchant continuous-wave shortage is an allocation problem at the integrated players rather than an industry yield problem. Coherent stating it does not foresee selling indium phosphide lasers externally is that allocation decision made explicit. That is bullish for the integrated names and materially less bullish for the small merchant suppliers positioned as the way to play it. Sivers remains the sharpest example of the gap between the two: a roughly sixfold share move during a quarter in which reported revenue fell 22% year on year and the company disclosed first-half revenue slipping into the second, with no numbers until 27 August.

digests.narrative:
The theme's error this month was treating memory as one bottleneck. It is two, and they are tightening for different reasons. DRAM and HBM are supply-set: TrendForce has server DRAM contract prices rising 13-18% quarter on quarter in 3Q26 with long-term agreements capping the increase, and HBM contract prices expected multiples higher in 2027 against RDIMM bit supply growing only 15-20% year on year. NAND is a separate market with its own enterprise-SSD driver. The desk had been holding only the NAND leg.

The scale on the DRAM side is now the largest single earnings event on this map. Micron's last reported quarter put revenue at $41.46B, against $23.86B the prior quarter and $9.30B a year earlier, with data centre alone above $25B — an annualised run-rate over $100B — and the following quarter guided near $50B. That is a fourfold revenue expansion in twelve months at a company whose product is a commodity, which is what a genuine supply constraint looks like when it is priced under contract rather than spot.

The policy layer added a second-order datapoint: Washington urging Apple away from Chinese memory, which on the analyst's own reading is happening while CXMT and YMTC are themselves raising prices. That matters less as a volume commitment than as evidence the cheap-Chinese-supply escape valve is not open. The discipline for this theme is that the exit signal is not a demand miss — it is the first quarter in which long-term agreement pricing stops rising.
keyPoints: DRAM/HBM and NAND are separate markets tightening for separate reasons — the desk now holds both legs

TrendForce: server DRAM contract prices +13-18% Q/Q in 3Q26, capped by long-term agreements
HBM contract prices expected multiples higher in 2027 against RDIMM bit supply growth of only 15-20%

digests.narrative:
The foundry layer is now the least ambiguous card on this map, because TSMC publishes monthly. July net revenue was NT$467.58B, up 44.7% year on year and 5.6% month on month, with January to July at NT$2,872.06B, up 37.0%. Monthly disclosure removes the argument that the AI order book is still a forecast — it is shipping. The limit is worth stating in the same breath: monthly revenue is a shipment number, not a capacity number, and it says nothing about how CoWoS allocation splits between the accelerator vendors, which is where the 2027 constraint actually sits.

The equipment leg confirmed it from the other side. Applied Materials reported record fiscal Q3 revenue of $9.12B, up 25%, with non-GAAP EPS of $3.50, up 41%, and guided fiscal Q4 to roughly $10.25B while raising its semiconductor systems expectations for calendar 2026. Then the stock fell about 5%. That is the pattern of the week across the whole chain — beat, raise, sell — and it is a margin and multiple story, not a demand story.

Intel and GlobalFoundries remain the quiet half of the card. Intel's disclosed 14A schedule is unchanged at risk production in 2027 and high volume in 2028, so external foundry revenue is not a near-term event. GlobalFoundries has produced no new evidence in three weeks; its CHIPS silicon-photonics award and named CPO customer list remain the whole case, and both are immaterial to a company that size.

digests.narrative:
Nebius set the bar for the layer: revenue of $582.3M, up 454% year on year and 46% sequentially, at roughly 50% adjusted AI-cloud EBITDA margin, with $8.04B of cash and its 2026 guidance reiterated at $3.0-3.4B revenue and $7-9B of year-end ARR. The signal the analyst pulled out is the more useful part — management saying it could sell its entire 2027 capacity on current terms. In a layer where most names market backlog, a capacity-sold-out statement is the harder claim.

The composition of this card changed this week. CleanSpark, Hut 8 and Riot move in from the triage bucket, because the distinction between a bitcoin miner and a neocloud has stopped being meaningful: what these companies actually own is powered land and grid interconnection, and they are converting it. Riot's multi-billion, multi-decade agreement with Anthropic, with an AMD option expansion alongside it, is the clearest example. Power capacity, not GPUs, is the scarce input in this layer.

The discipline the card needs is the one IREN keeps illustrating. Its last disclosure covers the March quarter — revenue $144.8M, of which AI Cloud Services was $33.6M — and it does not report until 16 September, while every move in the name this month came from someone else's filing. A theme priced on read-through rather than disclosure is how a sector gets ahead of itself, and this one is.

digests.narrative:
The substrate and test layer is where this book's firmest evidence sits, and it strengthened again without a substrate company reporting anything. Coherent doubling six-inch indium phosphide capacity ahead of plan is a direct read-through to AXT, which grows the substrate that capacity sits on and already holds reservation deposits of $43.5M from Lumentum and $22.3M from Coherent. Prepaid wafer capacity is the rational response to laser-layer pricing power, and none of it has been drawn down or cancelled.

Test is the quieter half and had the cleaner datapoint. AEHR took another $22M follow-on order for AI processor wafer-level burn-in from its lead customer — a repeat purchase from the same buyer, which is firmer evidence than most of what this layer runs on. FormFactor joins the card this week on its co-packaged optics systems commentary, where systems revenue nearly doubled on CPO growth; it is the test gate on the same ramp the photonics card is arguing about. Applied Materials guiding fiscal Q4 to roughly $10.25B after a record $9.12B quarter says the equipment feeding all of this is shipping.

Two housekeeping notes. LPKF has moved out of this card into glass, where its story belongs; glass substrate timelines are no longer read from here. And the critical-minerals thread — direct government investment into scandium, graphite, boron and magnet rare earths — continues to treat upstream inputs as strategic rather than commercial, with still no revenue attached at any listed name the desk tracks.

digests.narrative:
The layer's read-through hardened in one direction and went quiet in the other. The analyst's survey of this month's optical earnings places Broadcom inside the narrowed Western pool for first-generation co-packaged optics alongside Lumentum, Coherent and Sivers, while MACOM reads as a near-package rather than co-packaged participant and Semtech has shown nothing visible since its HieFo acquisition.

The layer's main claim is still the DSP and TIA bottleneck AOI flagged on its call — the signal-processing and amplifier silicon inside every transceiver — and it is still second-hand. The practical consequence is unchanged: transceiver revenue forecasts built purely on laser capacity understate the constraint chain, because a module needs the DSP and the TIA too.

No company disclosure from the named suppliers themselves, and no dedicated desk position. This remains a layer whose importance to the buildout is obvious and whose evidence is entirely other people's earnings calls.

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.

digests.narrative:
The card's largest name by score is not a company. Churchill Capital XI is a pre-close special purpose acquisition vehicle: the Agility Robotics combination was announced 24 June 2026 at roughly $2.5B, the Form S-4 was only confidentially submitted on 14 July, and closing still requires shareholder approval, SEC review, regulatory clearance and exchange listing, after which the ticker becomes AGLT. Digit is genuinely deployed at Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and Mercado Libre, but those are disclosed as programmes rather than volumes, so the per-robot compute, memory and lidar content that would justify a place on a hardware supply map is unquantified. The desk retired its verdict this week for that reason.

Tesla holds second place on this card as a scoring artefact rather than a thesis. Its mentions are almost entirely incidental name-drops inside multi-ticker recap posts, and the only recent one is a polysilicon post in which the analyst says he is not familiar with the supply chain he is describing. It is recorded as a pass specifically so it stops presenting as a conviction idea.

Conviction stays low, and it should. The humanoid thesis is real and early; what this card currently measures is enthusiasm about listing structures, not deployed units. The datapoint that would change it is disclosed unit economics — robots delivered, revenue per robot, compute per robot — from anyone.

digests.narrative:
Nothing has been reported by the largest name in this layer since Q1 FY27, and everything else on this map is written ahead of it. NVIDIA's last quarter was revenue $81.6B up 85%, data centre $75.2B up 92%, GAAP gross margin 74.9%, with the next quarter guided to $91.0B plus or minus 2% and landing 26 August. The line worth reading first is not revenue but gross margin: guiding 74.9% again means NVIDIA expects to absorb the HBM and advanced-packaging cost inflation its suppliers are booking as record results, without passing it through. If that holds, the supplier margin expansion the rest of this book owns is coming out of someone's pocket, and it is worth knowing whose.

The structural change this month was at AMD. Q2 revenue was a record $11.5B, up 50%, with data centre $6.7B, up 107% and 58% of the company, and the Instinct MI400 series including MI455X and MI430X launched in the quarter. Q3 is guided to about $13B at roughly 56% gross margin with data-centre AI guided to well over 100% growth. For a supply-chain map the launch matters more than the revenue: a second rack-scale accelerator family in the market turns HBM, substrate and optics pull-through into a two-vendor problem, which widens the customer base every supplier on this map sells into.

The margin gap between the two — roughly 56% against 74.9% — is the honest summary of the competitive position. AMD is winning volume at structurally worse economics. That is good for suppliers and ambiguous for AMD shareholders, and the two should not be conflated.

digests.narrative:
The demand layer keeps filing numbers that make the buildout hard to argue with. Alphabet reported Q2 revenue of $119.8B, up 24%, with Google Cloud at $24.8B, up 82% — an acceleration, not a plateau — while consolidated operating margin still expanded two points to 34%. Amazon reported net sales of $200.6B, up 20%, with AWS up 37%, its fastest growth in eighteen quarters, at a $169B annualised run-rate and $16.6B of segment operating income.

The cost of that is now visible in the cash statements rather than only in the guidance. Amazon's property and equipment purchases rose $66.1B year on year and trailing twelve-month free cash flow swung to a $7.6B outflow. Alphabet guided 2026 capital expenditure to $180-190B and said 2027 would increase significantly, then raised again. The equity question in this layer has moved from whether the revenue arrives to whether the depreciation is ever earned back, and that is a different risk with a different trigger.

Two things the desk should hold about the read-through. First, hyperscaler capex is not uniformly good news for this map: Alphabet serves a large share of its cloud growth on internal TPUs, so each of its capex dollars converts into less merchant GPU, HBM and optics demand than a neocloud's does. No primary source quantifies that split, so it stays a caution rather than a number. Second, Alibaba joins this card this week as the non-US compute buyer, pulling on the same memory and networking supply — and it reports the June quarter on 20 August, which is the next real datapoint in this layer.

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
